description: We'll have a clear plan, a focused scope and a friendly team.
summary:
Pixel Flame is a free web app that answers one question for any area: is this fire season normal?
NASA satellites have mapped active fires for 26 years, but the record is split between MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012), which count the same fires very differently. We harmonized NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20) into one consistent weekly record since November 2000, filling sensor gaps such as the November 2026 loss of S-NPP data. Tested on years the model never saw, MODIS predicts real VIIRS counts with a weekly correlation of 0.99 for Sudan and Nigeria.
Users pick a country, draw an area or enter coordinates, choose any period, and get a burning-activity calendar, anomalies against the historical normal, an early-warning level, a count of separate fires, the season's start and shift, similar past years, an 8-week outlook, data downloads and a one-page situation report.
This matters because emergency responders, firefighters and land managers need to know early when burning is abnormal so they can act before fires escalate, and scientists gain a 26-year record that stays consistent across sensors.
details:
Pixel Flame: is this fire season normal?

Live app: https://ahmhashem.github.io/Pixel_Flame/
Code and full method: https://github.com/AhmHashem/Pixel_Flame

Satellite fire maps show where fires are. They don’t say whether a season is unusual or what usually comes next. Pixel Flame uses 26 years of NASA fire detections to answer those questions for any area.

What it does

You pick a country (Sudan, Nigeria or Egypt in this demo), draw an area or enter a point and radius, and choose a period. You get:

  • A burning calendar by week or month, as raw counts or as anomalies against the historical norm.
  • An early warning for the last 7 days, compared with the same week in every year since 2000 and rated Normal, Elevated, High or Extreme. It also counts separate fires, since one fire can show up as many hotspots.
  • When the busy season usually starts, with a countdown.
  • Whether the season is shifting, comparing 2001–2010 with 2016–2025. A change only counts as clear if it’s bigger than normal year-to-year variation.
  • Similar past years, such as “Sudan’s 2026 so far looks most like 2004.”
  • An 8-week outlook with uncertainty ranges from the area’s own backtests.
  • Live hotspots with time since detection, fire power and directions.
  • Downloads (CSV, PNG) and a one-page report you can print or save as PDF.

On 14 November 2026, Nigeria rated High: 7,000 hotspots in the past week against a typical 3,155, with its usual season 19 days away.

Who it helps

Emergency teams can see whether this week is abnormal and how many separate fires are burning. Firefighters get live hotspots for their area. Land managers can see when the season starts and whether it’s shifting. Scientists get an open, documented method and the data behind it. The aim is a trustworthy answer to “is this fire season normal?”, early enough to act on.

How it works

MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012) see fires differently, so their raw counts can’t be compared. We:

  1. Collected NASA FIRMS archives for 2000–2025 and the live API for 2026.
  2. Kept vegetation fires only, removing gas flares, industrial heat and volcanoes, including in near-real-time data.
  3. Filled gaps. We found 69 days since 2012 when S-NPP recorded almost nothing while other satellites saw fires. Those days are filled from NOAA-20 or MODIS.
  4. Gridded detections into 0.25° cells, 52 weeks a year.
  5. Calibrated the sensors against each other, month by month, wherever they overlap.
  6. Tested on years the model never saw. Sudan and Nigeria hold up well, with weekly correlations of 0.99. Egypt doesn’t: its correlation is 0.57 and it runs 36% low, because most of its burning is small agricultural fires that MODIS rarely detects. Its earlier years are flagged as low quality throughout the app.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib) for the pipeline. JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web app, with Leaflet and Leaflet.draw for the map and Apache ECharts for charts. Headless Chrome for end-to-end tests, and a colour-vision palette validator. Git, GitHub, GitHub Pages and Codespaces. Claude Code as an AI coding assistant. No special hardware: it runs on a laptop and in a browser, and the static site is free to host and works on a phone.

What’s creative

It turns a map of dots into an answer with context. It counts fires, not just hotspots, by merging neighbouring detections. It uses circular statistics so seasons that run across New Year, like Sudan’s October to February season, are measured correctly. It finds similar past years so users can see how comparable seasons ended. And it keeps working through satellite outages by switching sensors automatically.

What we considered

  • Sensor differences: pixel size, overpass times, and the orbit drift of Terra and Aqua, which is why MODIS is calibrated to VIIRS using 2012–2020 only.
  • Data gaps and false detections: outages, gas flares, industrial heat and volcanoes.
  • Honest validation: weak results, like Egypt’s, are shown and flagged rather than hidden.
  • Honest uncertainty: outlook ranges come from real backtests, and similar years are historical comparisons, not forecasts.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe colours, light and dark modes, phone layouts, and printable reports.
  • Different fire types: savanna burning in Sudan and Nigeria, and Egypt’s small agricultural fires as a hard case.

Limits

  • Area statistics use 0.25° cells, so custom edges are accurate to about 25 km. The hotspot CSV uses your exact area.
  • Recent months use near-real-time data until NASA publishes standard processing.
  • A hotspot marks the centre of a satellite pixel, not a confirmed fire front. The outlook and similar years are statistical, not predictions of individual fires.

Next steps

Extend to every country, send automatic alerts when an area turns High, and add burned-area and fire-weather data.
